Refinancing: calculate the real benefit

A practical starting point for Hong Kong homebuyers and mortgage holders.

Start with the mortgage you actually have

Use your latest outstanding balance and the number of months left, rather than the original loan amount or original term. Obtain a redemption quotation from your existing bank. It should identify early repayment charges, cashback clawbacks and any discharge fees.

Separate cash flow from borrowing cost

A lower monthly payment can result from a longer repayment term. That can leave you with more debt later, even if the immediate payment feels easier. Our refinancing calculator holds the remaining term constant to make the rate comparison meaningful.

It calculates net benefit as interest avoided over your chosen horizon, less legal fees, penalties and cashback clawbacks, plus new cashback assumed to be retained. Principal repayments are not treated as a borrowing cost. A positive result is an estimate under the inputs, not a guarantee.

A worked example

Assume a HK$4 million balance, 20 years remaining, a 4% current rate, a 3% new rate and HK$10,000 switching costs with no cashback. Monthly payments fall from about HK$24,239 to HK$22,184. Over 24 months, estimated interest savings are about HK$78,000, giving a net benefit of about HK$68,000 after costs. Both rates are held constant. Actual offers and daily interest calculations can differ.

Check the horizon and conditions

  • Set the comparison horizon to how long you realistically expect to retain the new mortgage.
  • Confirm when cashback is paid and when it must be repaid.
  • Include all fees and insurance changes. This tool assumes costs and cashback occur at outset.
  • Check the net benefit as well as first cost recovery. An initial cashback benefit can disappear later if the new rate is higher.
  • Ask how the result changes if the floating rate rises or the valuation falls.

Our first-recovery figure is the first month in which cumulative interest savings cover net switching costs. It may differ from a simple fees-divided-by-monthly-payment-savings calculation because principal repayment patterns also change.
